sources.entry: Atalaya - Watch and maintain Linux servers over SSH: live dashboard, Docker containers, systemd services, your own scripts, package updates and files over SFTP, with nothing installed on the server.

summary.one_liner: Atalaya is a macOS app that monitors and manages Linux servers over SSH, with nothing installed on the server side.
summary.what_it_does: It logs into a Linux server over SSH and shows a live dashboard of CPU, memory, load, temperature, network and disks, with user-arrangeable cards. It lists Docker containers with their state and offers start, stop, restart and log viewing. It lists systemd services with plain-language descriptions and finds .sh scripts in the home folder, shown as buttons that stream their output, with descriptions taken from comments inside the scripts. It groups available package updates (security, kernel, programs, libraries) so you choose what to install, and it browses files over SFTP with upload, download, preview, rename and delete. It can also install a Docker Compose project from a repository after checking images, ports and conflicts, and it supports several servers as tabs.
use_cases: monitor a home or remote Linux server from a Mac
view and restart Docker containers on a server
check systemd service status over SSH
run maintenance scripts from a menu bar app
apply selected Linux package updates remotely
transfer files to and from a server via SFTP
deploy a Docker Compose project to a server
how_to_run: Download Atalaya-1.0.0.zip from the Releases page (not the source zip), unzip it and drag Atalaya.app to Applications
Right-click the app, choose Open, then Open again to bypass the first-run block
Add a server with host, user, and either a password or SSH key
Build from source: git clone the repository, cd atalaya, run ./build.sh
Optionally run Tools/setup-signing.sh to create a stable local signing identity before building
stack: Swift (implied by macOS app and build script)
notable: Requires nothing installed on the monitored server: no agent, daemon, web panel or open port
Stores passwords in the macOS Keychain rather than a file
Uses ~/.ssh/known_hosts to trust only known host keys
Turns .sh scripts in the home folder into one-click buttons, explained by their own comments
Checks for new releases once a day but never installs anything automatically
caveats: App is signed but not notarised by Apple, so the first launch needs right-click Open
Sudo is needed for system updates, service restarts and shutdown; Docker features need the user in the docker group
